title: Ecosystems and Biomes
description: What ecosystems are, how they're organised, and Earth's major biomes

concepts.title: What Is an Ecosystem?
concepts.contentHtml:
An ecosystem is all the living organisms in a particular area (biotic components) plus the non-living physical environment they interact with (abiotic components: sunlight, temperature, water, soil chemistry).

Ecosystems can be as large as the Amazon rainforest or as small as a garden pond. What defines them is the flow of energy and cycling of matter among their components.

Eugene Odum, who pioneered ecosystem ecology in the 1950s, likened an ecosystem to a machine with inputs (energy, nutrients) and outputs (heat, exported matter). Understanding ecosystems as integrated systems — not just collections of species — transformed ecology from natural history into a quantitative science.

concepts.title: Biomes
concepts.contentHtml:
A biome is a large-scale ecosystem characterised by a dominant vegetation type and climate.

  • Tropical rainforest: ~2,500 mm rain/year, ~25°C; highest biodiversity on Earth
  • Temperate deciduous forest: seasonal, cold winters, moderate rain
  • Grassland/savanna: seasonal drought prevents tree dominance; large grazing mammals
  • Desert: <250 mm rain/year; extreme adaptations (e.g. cacti with succulent stems)
  • Tundra: permafrost, short growing season, dominated by low-lying plants
  • Taiga: boreal conifer forest; world's largest terrestrial biome

Biome boundaries are determined primarily by temperature and precipitation, not by geography per se.

concepts.title: Abiotic Factors and Limiting Resources
concepts.contentHtml:
Liebig's Law of the Minimum (1840) states that plant growth is limited by whichever nutrient is in shortest supply — not by total resources. Nitrogen and phosphorus are most often limiting in terrestrial ecosystems; iron in open ocean.

Adding a limiting nutrient causes rapid growth — but also potential problems. Eutrophication occurs when excess nitrogen or phosphorus (from fertiliser runoff) floods into a lake, causing algal blooms that deplete oxygen when they decompose, killing fish.

Light, temperature, water, and soil pH are all abiotic factors that shape which species can survive in a location. Every species has a range of tolerance for each factor — its ecological niche.

title: Energy Flow and Food Webs
description: How energy moves through ecosystems and why there are so few top predators

concepts.title: Producers, Consumers, and Decomposers
concepts.contentHtml:
Every ecosystem has a trophic structure. Producers (autotrophs) capture energy — plants use photosynthesis; some bacteria use chemosynthesis (hydrothermal vents).

Consumers (heterotrophs) obtain energy by eating: herbivores eat plants (primary consumers), carnivores eat animals (secondary, tertiary consumers), omnivores eat both.

Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead organic matter, releasing nutrients back into the soil and water. Without decomposers, nutrients would be locked in dead bodies and all life would grind to a halt. The forest floor's rich soil is essentially decomposer output.

concepts.title: The 10% Rule and Energy Pyramids
concepts.contentHtml:
Energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient. On average, only about 10% of energy from one level is incorporated into the next — the rest is lost as heat through respiration. This is the 10% rule (or Lindeman's efficiency, 1942).

A grass field with 10,000 kJ of energy supports ~1,000 kJ of grasshopper biomass, ~100 kJ of frog biomass, ~10 kJ of snake biomass, and just ~1 kJ of hawk biomass. This is why energy pyramids taper sharply and why top predators are rare.

Eating lower on the food chain is more energetically efficient — one reason vegetarian diets have a smaller ecological footprint.

concepts.title: Food Web Complexity and Keystone Species
concepts.contentHtml:
Real ecosystems have complex food webs rather than simple chains: most animals eat multiple species and are eaten by multiple predators. This complexity confers stability — removing one species often has limited impact if others can fill its role.

But some species are keystone species — disproportionately important relative to their abundance. The sea otter is a classic example: studies by James Estes and colleagues from the 1970s showed that sea otters control sea urchin populations, which in turn control kelp forests. Remove otters → urchin explosion → kelp destruction → entire ecosystem collapses.

The reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone in 1995 triggered a 'trophic cascade' that even changed river courses by reducing elk grazing on riverbanks.

title: Nutrient Cycles
description: How carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus cycle through the biosphere

concepts.title: The Carbon Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Carbon moves between living organisms, the atmosphere, oceans, and geological reservoirs. Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the atmosphere; respiration and decomposition return it. Combustion of fossil fuels adds CO2 that was sequestered over millions of years.

The ocean is the largest active carbon reservoir — it absorbs ~25% of human CO2 emissions. As CO2 dissolves, it forms carbonic acid, lowering ocean pH (ocean acidification). Since the Industrial Revolution, ocean pH has dropped from ~8.2 to ~8.1 — small in absolute terms but huge in chemical terms because pH is logarithmic.

Coral reefs are particularly vulnerable to acidification because they build calcium carbonate skeletons that dissolve in acidic water.

concepts.title: The Nitrogen Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Nitrogen gas (N2) makes up 78% of the atmosphere but is unusable by most organisms. Nitrogen fixation converts N2 into ammonia (NH3) — done by specialised bacteria including Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes and free-living cyanobacteria.

Fixed nitrogen is incorporated into amino acids and proteins. Decomposers return it to ammonium; nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrate; denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate back to N2, completing the cycle.

The Haber-Bosch process (industrial nitrogen fixation) has doubled the amount of reactive nitrogen in the biosphere since ~1900, enabling global food production — but also causing widespread eutrophication and N2O emissions (a potent greenhouse gas).

concepts.title: The Phosphorus Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Phosphorus has no significant atmospheric phase — it cycles through rock, soil, water, and organisms. Rocks are slowly weathered by rain and biological activity, releasing phosphate (PO4³⁻) into soils and rivers.

Plants absorb phosphate for DNA, ATP, and cell membranes. Animals get it by eating plants. When organisms die, decomposers release phosphate back to the soil. Some phosphorus sinks to ocean sediments and is only returned to land through geological uplift — a very slow process.

Phosphorus is a finite resource: global phosphate rock reserves may be depleted within ~100–300 years at current mining rates. This 'peak phosphorus' problem is as serious as climate change for long-term food security, yet far less discussed.

title: Population Ecology
description: How populations grow, crash, and reach equilibrium

concepts.title: Exponential and Logistic Growth
concepts.contentHtml:
In unlimited conditions, populations grow exponentially — doubling each generation. Charles Darwin noted that even slow-breeding elephants could produce 19 million descendants in 750 years if all survived.

Real populations face resource limits. Logistic growth describes populations that start exponentially but slow as they approach the environment's carrying capacity (K) — the maximum population a habitat can sustain.

The S-shaped (sigmoidal) logistic growth curve is a better approximation of real populations. But carrying capacity is not fixed: it changes with climate, resource availability, and human modification of habitats.

concepts.title: Predator-Prey Dynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
Predator and prey populations often oscillate in linked cycles. The classic example: Canadian lynx and snowshoe hare data from Hudson's Bay Company fur records (1845–1935) show 10-year population cycles where hare peaks are followed by lynx peaks, then crashes.

The Lotka-Volterra equations (developed independently in the 1920s) model these cycles mathematically. The logic: more hares → more food for lynx → lynx increase → more hares eaten → hares decline → lynx starve → lynx decline → hares recover.

Real systems are more complex — hare cycles are also driven by vegetation, not just predators. But the model captures the essential feedback loop.

concepts.title: r- and K-Selected Species
concepts.contentHtml:
Species differ dramatically in their reproductive strategies. r-selected species (r = intrinsic growth rate) invest in producing many small offspring quickly with little parental care: bacteria, insects, annual plants, weeds. They thrive in unpredictable, disturbed environments.

K-selected species produce few, well-cared-for offspring and invest heavily in each one: elephants, great apes, whales. They are well-adapted to stable environments near carrying capacity but are slow to recover from population declines.

This r/K continuum explains vulnerability to extinction: K-selected species with slow reproduction (like giant pandas or blue whales) cannot rebound quickly from hunting or habitat loss.

title: Biodiversity and Conservation
description: Why biodiversity matters, what threatens it, and how we protect it

concepts.title: Measuring and Valuing Biodiversity
concepts.contentHtml:
Biodiversity has three levels: genetic diversity (variation within a species), species diversity (number and evenness of species in an area), and ecosystem diversity (variety of habitat types).

Species diversity is measured by species richness (raw count) and evenness (how equal the abundances are). The Shannon index combines both.

Biodiversity provides ecosystem services: pollination (worth ~$235 billion/year globally), water purification, climate regulation, soil formation, and medicines. Roughly a quarter of prescription drugs were originally derived from plants. The economic value of biodiversity vastly exceeds the cost of protecting it.

concepts.title: The Sixth Mass Extinction
concepts.contentHtml:
Current extinction rates are estimated at 100–1,000 times the background rate — driven by habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution, and climate change. Scientists call this the Sixth Mass Extinction or the Holocene extinction.

The IUCN Red List tracks species status: over 44,000 of the 157,000 assessed species are threatened. Habitat destruction is the leading driver — the Amazon has lost ~20% of its original cover; >50% of global wetlands have been destroyed since 1900.

Island biogeography theory (MacArthur and Wilson, 1967) predicts that species number is a function of island area and isolation. Habitat fragmentation creates 'islands' of natural habitat, reducing species richness predictably.

concepts.title: Conservation Strategies
concepts.contentHtml:
Effective conservation uses multiple tools. Protected areas (national parks, marine reserves) cover ~17% of land and ~8% of ocean, but placement, management quality, and connectivity matter as much as coverage.

Biological corridors connect fragmented habitats, allowing migration and gene flow. The Yellowstone to Yukon initiative aims to create a 3,000-km corridor for large mammals.

Ex situ conservation (zoos, seed banks, cryopreservation) is a last resort. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds ~1.4 million seed samples from almost every country — an insurance policy against crop extinction.

The CBD's 30×30 target (30% of land and ocean protected by 2030) and E.O. Wilson's 'Half-Earth' proposal reflect the scale of action ecologists argue is necessary.

title: Community Ecology
description: Species interactions and how communities assemble

concepts.title: Interaction Types
concepts.contentHtml:
Species interact in characteristic ways. Predation (one eats the other), competition (both lose access to a resource), mutualism (both benefit — pollination, mycorrhizae), commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected), parasitism (one benefits at the other's expense without immediate killing).

Each interaction shapes population dynamics and community structure. Strong interactions are often surprisingly few — many species coexist with weak interactions.

concepts.title: Keystone Species
concepts.contentHtml:
Some species have outsized effects on their communities relative to their abundance. Keystone species like sea otters (controlling sea urchins, allowing kelp forests), wolves (regulating elk, allowing forest regrowth in Yellowstone), and starfish (preventing mussel monoculture) maintain ecosystem structure.

Remove a keystone species and the community can transform dramatically. The kelp forest collapses; the riparian forest disappears; the mussel bed takes over.

Reintroduction successes: Yellowstone wolves (1995) reshaped river morphology by changing elk grazing — a textbook trophic cascade.

concepts.title: Niche & Coexistence
concepts.contentHtml:
A species' niche is its 'role' — combined resources used, conditions tolerated, and effects on environment. The competitive exclusion principle (Gause): two species with identical niches can't coexist; one will outcompete the other.

Real species have differentiated niches via resource partitioning, temporal segregation, or spatial segregation. Tropical rainforests pack thousands of species into apparent overlap — actual niche differentiation is subtle.

The Lotka-Volterra equations formalize competition and predation dynamics — staples of theoretical ecology since the 1920s.

concepts.title: Reference States
concepts.contentHtml:
Restoration aims to return a degraded ecosystem to a more natural state. The reference: a comparable healthy ecosystem, historical records, or a representative undegraded site.

Goals vary: full pre-disturbance state (often impossible), functional restoration (services, processes), or 'novel ecosystems' that work despite changed species mixes.

concepts.title: Practical Approaches
concepts.contentHtml:
Reforestation. Wetland restoration (bringing water back, removing levees, replanting). Stream daylighting (uncovering buried streams). Invasive species removal. Reintroducing extirpated species.

Costanza-style payments for ecosystem services support restoration economically. Often restoration costs less than damage prevention would have, but takes decades to centuries to fully manifest.

concepts.title: Rewilding
concepts.contentHtml:
Rewilding reintroduces ecosystem-engineering species — large herbivores, top predators — to restore self-regulating ecological dynamics.

Yellowstone wolves (1995) — kept elk moving, allowed willows to regrow, brought beavers back, changed river morphology. European bison reintroduced to Romania, Netherlands. Iberian lynx recovery. Tasmanian devil reintroductions on the Australian mainland.

De-extinction (mammoth via genome editing, thylacine, others) is at the speculative frontier. Whether such species would integrate into modern ecosystems is unresolved.

title: Climate, Tipping Points & Adaptation
description: Ecology in a rapidly changing world

concepts.title: Range Shifts and Phenology
concepts.contentHtml:
Species are shifting poleward and upslope as climate warms. Average range shift: ~17 km per decade poleward, ~11 m upslope per decade.

Phenological shifts: spring events (flowering, hatching, migration arrival) are happening earlier. About 60% of studied species show shifts; many are mismatched with their ecological partners (pollinators, prey).

Some species can keep up; others can't. Mountain endemics with no higher to go are particularly at risk. Polar bears, alpine pika, and many salamanders face range collapse.

concepts.title: Tipping Points
concepts.contentHtml:
Ecosystems can change suddenly when stressors push them past a threshold. Examples: Sahel drying. Coral reefs to algae-dominated states. Lakes to eutrophic regimes. Tropical forests to savanna.

Tipping points are often hysteretic — even when conditions improve, the new state can persist. Coral reefs once shifted to algae are very hard to restore.

Climate tipping elements (Arctic ice, Amazon dieback, AMOC slowdown, permafrost methane) interact and may cascade. The 1.5 °C target was largely set with these risks in mind.

concepts.title: Conservation in a Warming World
concepts.contentHtml:
Conservation must now plan for moving climate envelopes. Static reserves protect against habitat loss but not climate change. Conservation corridors let species track shifting climates.

Assisted migration — moving species ahead of climate shifts — is controversial but increasingly considered for endangered species. Whitebark pine, monarch butterflies, oysters have all been candidates.

Ecosystem-based adaptation (mangroves for coastal protection, urban green space for cooling) explicitly uses biodiversity to mitigate climate impacts. Both biodiversity and human well-being benefit.
